claims.text: Organic produce carries lower pesticide residues than conventional produce
claims.note: Twenty years of state monitoring: about 76% of fresh organic samples had no detectable residue in 2021, and average residues were 0.002 mg/kg for organic fruit and vegetables against 0.40-0.48 mg/kg for conventional, a gap repeated every year since 2014.

claims.text: Washing produce removes most pesticide residue
claims.note: Rinsing and baking-soda soaks remove part of surface residues, but systemic and absorbed residues stay in the produce.

claims.text: Organic farming uses no pesticides
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.206(e) lets organic producers apply biological or botanical substances or National List synthetics to control pests, weeds and diseases when cultural, mechanical and physical methods are not enough, so organic farming does use pesticides.

claims.text: Switching to an organic diet quickly lowers pesticide levels in the body
claims.note: All four whole-diet crossover trials (children and adults) that measured urinary pesticide metabolites found significant drops, up to 90%, within a few days of switching to organic.

claims.text: Glyphosate residues in food harm human health
claims.note: EFSA's 2023 peer review put the maximum chronic dietary intake of glyphosate at 3% of the ADI (Dutch toddlers) and acute intake at 2% of the ARfD; provisional, limited to the EU's representative uses, but an independent regulator finding dietary residues far below levels of concern.

claims.text: Organic farming supports more biodiversity on the farm than conventional farming
claims.note: Meta-analyses find roughly a third more species richness on organic farms on average, varying by taxon and landscape.

claims.text: Imported organic food is less trustworthy than domestic organic food
claims.note: The largest documented organic fraud cases involved imported grain, though imports must meet the same rules and enforcement tightened under the 2023 SOE rule.

claims.text: Regulators assess pesticides one at a time and ignore combined effects of residue mixtures
claims.note: EFSA ran a cumulative risk assessment of dietary residues, adding doses across pesticides with a common effect and computing a combined margin of exposure at each percentile, so EU regulators do assess combined effects within effect groups.

claims.text: Pesticide exposure causes cancer in people
claims.note: High occupational exposure to some pesticides is linked to cancers such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma, but evidence at dietary exposure levels is weak.

claims.text: Organic standards require higher animal welfare than conventional farming
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.238-205.239 set welfare rules, among them year-round outdoor access, no continuous total confinement, bans on gestation and farrowing crates, de-beaking and induced molting, and conditions allowing freedom of movement; the regulation does not itself compare these with conventional practice or say how they are enforced.

claims.text: Organic labelling is mainly a marketing tool to charge higher prices
claims.note: The organic label is a legally enforced production standard with inspections and real input restrictions, even though it is heavily marketed.

claims.text: Most people carry detectable glyphosate in their urine
claims.note: In nationally representative NHANES samples, glyphosate was detected in the urine of 81.2% (2013-2014), 70.0% (2015-2016) and 81.7% (2017-2018) of the U.S. population aged 3 and up, though concentrations fell 38% over the period.

claims.text: Organic food is more nutritious than conventional food
claims.note: Crop vitamins and minerals are similar under both systems; organic has modestly more phenolics and its dairy about 50% more omega-3, but the review calls established nutritional differences small with no strong health conclusions.

claims.text: Organic crops contain more antioxidants and polyphenols than conventional crops
claims.note: Meta-analysis of 343 publications found phenolic acids, flavanones, stilbenes, flavones, flavonols and anthocyanins 19-69% higher in organic crops, with moderate-to-good GRADE reliability for most, despite very high heterogeneity.

claims.text: Organic crops contain less cadmium than conventional crops
claims.note: Weighted and unweighted meta-analyses both found significantly lower Cd in organic crops (mean difference -48%, wide CI), significant for cereals but not fruit or vegetables separately; GRADE reliability moderate.

claims.text: Eating organic food lowers cancer risk
claims.note: In 623,080 UK women followed 9.3 years (53,769 cancers), usually/always eating organic food was not linked to lower total cancer (RR 1.03, 0.99-1.07; 1.00 among consistent consumers), breast cancer was slightly higher (RR 1.09), and only NHL was lower (RR 0.79), which the authors say may be chance.

claims.text: Eating more fruit and vegetables matters more than whether they are organic
claims.note: Produce intake has large, consistent health associations, while residue risks at typical levels are small and unproven.

claims.text: Organic food is especially important for children and pregnant women
claims.note: Children's higher intake per body weight and developmental sensitivity are real, but no trial shows a health benefit from organic diets at residue levels.

claims.text: Pre-harvest glyphosate spraying leaves higher residues in oats, grains and legumes
claims.note: Desiccant use close to harvest is the main reason conventional oats and pulses test higher for glyphosate, usually still within legal limits.

claims.text: Dietary pesticide residues alter the human gut microbiome
claims.note: Animal studies and one small observational twin study suggest effects, but there is no causal human evidence.

claims.text: Buying organic matters less for produce with thick inedible peels
claims.note: Peeled produce such as avocados, onions and bananas shows low residues in the edible part even when grown conventionally.

claims.text: The organic label does not mean food is free of heavy metals
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.203 only requires managing inputs so they do not add to heavy-metal contamination, and the 205.671 residue exclusion covers prohibited substances; the excerpt sets no heavy-metal limit for organic food.

claims.text: Rice-based foods carry more inorganic arsenic than most other foods
claims.note: Rice takes up arsenic from flooded paddies far more than other grains, which is why FDA set a specific limit for infant rice cereal.

claims.text: Organic food costs substantially more than conventional food
claims.note: Hedonic model on 2004-10 Nielsen Homescan purchases, controlling for package, brand, store and market, found positive organic premiums for all 17 products, above 20% for 16 of them (2010: 7% spinach to 82% eggs); meat and poultry were not covered.

claims.text: Pesticide residues on conventional produce are too low to harm health
claims.note: For the ten most detected pesticides on each 2010 Dirty Dozen crop, RfDs exceeded mean exposure in every case and by over 1000-fold in more than 90% of comparisons; limited to 2004-2008 data, top-ten pesticides and mean (not high-end) exposure.

claims.text: Organic farming needs more land to produce the same amount of food
claims.note: Meta-analysis of within-publication LCA pairs found organic systems need 25-110% more land per unit of food (p<0.001, n=37), driven by mismatched manure nutrient release and lower yields; mostly high-input Europe/North America systems.

claims.text: Organic farming improves soil health
claims.note: Long-term trials show higher soil organic matter and biological activity under organic management, partly from manure and compost inputs.

claims.text: Organic farming yields less food per acre than conventional farming
claims.note: Hierarchical meta-analysis of 115 studies (1071 comparisons, 38 countries) found organic yields 19.2% lower (95% CI 15.5-22.9%), with conventional higher for all crop types; the authors note publication bias may overstate the gap.

claims.text: The Dirty Dozen list is a reliable guide to which produce to buy organic
claims.note: The 2010 EWG method ignored food consumption and toxicological thresholds and was skewed toward counts of multiple residues, so it could not rank risk (blueberries, cherries and kale had all exposures over 30,000-fold below RfDs); EWG has since added a toxicity factor but still no consumption weighting.

claims.text: Organic farming is better for the environment than conventional farming
claims.note: Per unit of food, organic used 15% less energy but needed 25-110% more land and had 37% higher eutrophication, with similar GHG and acidification; the authors say this does not make conventional more sustainable given its pesticide and nutrient inputs, which they could not measure.

claims.text: Many leading organic brands are owned by large conventional food companies
claims.note: Well-known US organic brands are owned by General Mills, Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, Kellogg, Danone and similar firms.

claims.text: Organic farms are inspected by an accredited certifier at least once a year
claims.note: Operations must hold a certificate from a USDA-accredited third-party certifier, and certifiers inspect all certified operations at least once each year.

claims.text: Most organic certification inspections are announced in advance
claims.note: The SOE rule requires unannounced inspections of only at least 5 percent of operations, beside the annual on-site inspections, which implies the routine annual inspection is usually scheduled; the fact sheet does not say this outright.

claims.text: Organic certification requires grazing animals to have access to pasture
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.237(c) requires ruminants to graze through the whole grazing season, at least 120 days a year, and to get on average at least 30 percent of their dry matter intake from pasture.

claims.text: Organic processed foods are no healthier than their conventional counterparts
claims.note: Organic snacks and cereals have similar sugar, fat and calories to conventional versions; the seal certifies ingredients' farming, not the product's nutrition.

claims.text: Organic enforcement is too weak to deter fraud
claims.note: Oversight gaps enabled major import fraud cases, but the 2023 Strengthening Organic Enforcement rule expanded certification and traceability requirements.

claims.text: Eating organic food has proven health benefits for the people who eat it
claims.note: The review concludes the link between organic food and health is insufficiently documented and that it is not possible to tell whether organic food plays a causal role in observed lower allergy, obesity or NHL, given residual confounding.

claims.text: USDA Organic prohibits genetically engineered ingredients
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.105(e) says organic products must be made without excluded methods (the regulation's term for genetic engineering), the one exception being approved vaccines; 205.301(f)(1) applies the same rule to every ingredient labeled organic.

claims.text: Much organic meat and dairy comes from large industrial-scale operations
claims.note: A large share of US organic milk and eggs comes from operations with thousands of animals, though they must meet pasture and outdoor rules.

claims.text: Organic farming bans all synthetic pesticides
claims.note: Annex I of EU Regulation 2021/1165 authorises plant protection active substances for organic production including paraffin oils, lime sulphur, copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, Bordeaux mixture and the synthetic pyrethroids deltamethrin and lambda-cyhalothrin (in traps only), so EU organic rules do not ban all synthetic pesticides.

claims.text: Pesticides allowed in organic farming are not necessarily safer than synthetic ones
claims.note: Most EU organic-approved pesticides are of low concern (none classed as suspected carcinogens or reproductive toxicants vs 27 and 26 among all approved), but pyrethrins share the pyrethroid mechanism and copper is toxic at high intake and ecotoxic, so some are not safer.

claims.text: Organic food is worth its price premium for health reasons
claims.note: Organic reliably lowers residue exposure, but no health outcome benefit has been shown to justify the premium on health grounds alone.

claims.text: Organic livestock cannot be given antibiotics or added growth hormones
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.238(c) says no animal treated with antibiotics, nor its products, may be sold as organic, and it bars hormones for growth, production or reproduction (205.237(b) also bars growth hormones and antibiotic-laced feed); sick animals must still be treated and then lose organic status.

claims.text: Land must be free of prohibited substances for three years before its crops can be certified organic
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.202(b) requires that no prohibited substance was applied to the field for 3 years before harvest of a crop sold as organic.

claims.text: Small farms can be organic in practice without being certified
claims.note: Certification costs and paperwork lead some small growers to farm organically uncertified; operations under 5,000 dollars in sales are exempt.

claims.text: Organic food costs more mainly because organic farming costs more to produce
claims.note: Higher labour, lower yields, certification and separate supply chains raise costs, but retail markups on organic often exceed the cost gap.

claims.text: The grass-fed label lets producers set their own definition
claims.note: USDA withdrew its grass-fed marketing standard in 2016; FSIS approves label claims case by case on producer documentation.

claims.text: Organic beef and dairy can come from grain-fed animals
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.239(d) calls organic ruminant slaughter stock 'typically grain finished' and allows feedlot finishing for up to one-fifth of the animal's life or 120 days, exempt from the 30 percent grazing rule; up to 70 percent of a ruminant's dry matter may be fed even during the grazing season (205.237(c)), provided the feed is organic.

claims.text: Cage-free and free-range labels say little about how hens actually live
claims.note: USDA free-range requires only some outdoor access and cage-free only no cages, with no space, duration or outdoor-quality minimums.

claims.text: Pasture-raised is an unregulated term with no required outdoor standard
claims.note: USDA has no codified pasture-raised standard; meaning depends on producer claims unless a third-party certification backs it.

claims.text: Grass-fed beef has a healthier fat profile than grain-fed beef
claims.note: Cited controlled experiment: switching beef from grain to grass finishing raised intramuscular PUFA 45%, n-3 PUFA over 3-fold, EPA over 5-fold and DHA 129%, with no change in n-6; forage diets also lower SFA in meat.

claims.text: Regenerative Organic Certified sets stricter standards than USDA Organic for soil, animal welfare and labour
claims.note: ROC requires USDA Organic as a baseline and adds soil-health, animal-welfare and farmworker-fairness requirements.

claims.text: The "natural" label has little regulatory meaning
claims.note: FDA has never formally defined 'natural' and has only an informal policy (nothing artificial or synthetic added) that does not address pesticides, processing or health; FSIS's meat definition (no artificial ingredients, minimally processed) likewise says nothing about how the animal was raised.

claims.text: Organic food tastes better than conventional food
claims.note: Blind taste tests show no consistent preference for organic; label-aware tests show a halo effect.

claims.text: Organic produce carries a higher risk of bacterial contamination than conventional produce
claims.note: The Stanford meta-analysis found no significant difference in E. coli contamination between organic and conventional produce.

claims.text: The USDA Organic seal requires at least 95 percent organic ingredients
claims.note: Products labeled 'organic' must contain at least 95 percent organic ingredients by weight, excluding water and salt (205.301(b)), and only '100 percent organic' and 'organic' products may carry the USDA seal (205.303(a)(4)).

claims.text: Products labelled "made with organic" ingredients need only 70 percent organic content
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.301(c) requires 'made with organic (specified ingredients)' products to contain at least 70 percent organic ingredients, excluding water and salt.

claims.text: Organic milk and meat contain more omega-3 fatty acids than conventional milk and meat
claims.note: Meta-analysis of 170 studies on cow's milk: weighted analysis found total n-3 PUFA 56% higher in organic milk (ALA +68%, EPA +67%, DPA +45%), GRADE moderate, robust across sensitivity analyses.

claims.text: The omega-3 advantage of organic milk and meat comes from grass feeding, not organic certification
claims.note: Redundancy analysis of a cross-European farm survey tied milk n-3 differences to grazing vs concentrate feeding, and conventional farms on low-input grazing diets sat in nearly the same position as organic farms.

claims.text: Organic meat carries fewer antibiotic-resistant bacteria than conventional meat
claims.note: Organic pork and chicken are less likely to harbour resistant bacteria, resistance is less common in organic pigs in four countries, and converting poultry farms to organic cut resistant Salmonella; MRSA differences lost significance after adjustment.

claims.text: Imported organic products must meet the same standards as domestic organic products
claims.note: Imports may be certified under foreign equivalency arrangements that need only be 'at least equivalent', not identical; OIG found 25 procedural and 9 technical differences in one arrangement and 68 and 28 in another, with no documented resolution of all of them.

claims.text: Fear of pesticide residues discourages people from eating fruit and vegetables
claims.note: One survey experiment found low-income shoppers less willing to buy produce after residue messaging; real-world effects are unmeasured.

claims.text: The extra omega-3 in organic milk and meat is too small to matter for health
claims.note: Switching to organic dairy and meat would raise dietary omega-3 by an estimated 2.5-8% and 2.5-4%; the review calls the effect minor with no specific health benefits derivable.

claims.text: Organic rules rest on an appeal to nature rather than evidence of best practice
claims.note: This is a framing judgment about the philosophy behind organic standards.

claims.text: Organic certification sets no living-condition rules for laying hens
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.238 applies to all organic livestock, poultry included: it requires housing that limits disease and conditions allowing exercise, freedom of movement and lower stress, and it bans de-beaking, beak trimming after 10 days and induced molting (the avian living-conditions section 205.241 is not in this excerpt).

claims.text: Animal Welfare Approved certification sets stronger hen welfare standards than USDA egg labels
claims.note: AWA requires pasture access, space minimums and bans beak cutting, well beyond USDA cage-free, free-range or organic rules.

claims.text: Knowing and trusting the farmer can replace organic certification
claims.note: Whether personal trust substitutes for third-party verification is a judgment about the buyer's values and knowledge.

claims.text: The organic seal is most useful when buyers cannot know the farm
claims.note: This is shopping advice about when third-party verification adds value.

claims.text: Organic dairy cows emit more methane than conventional dairy cows
claims.note: Forage-heavy diets raise methane per unit of milk in many studies, but per-cow and per-farm comparisons are mixed.

claims.text: The USDA organic standard has been watered down as large companies entered organic
claims.note: Hydroponic certification and the 2018 withdrawal of the animal welfare rule are cited as weakening, but other rules such as pasture and enforcement were tightened.

claims.text: USDA Organic standards do not protect farmworker welfare
claims.note: The National Organic Program regulates inputs and practices, not labour conditions or wages.

claims.text: Regenerative organic farming yields far more than industrial agriculture
claims.note: Even with diversification practices (organic polycultures or more rotations) the organic yield gap shrank to 9% and 8% but did not reverse; no setting showed organic yielding far more than conventional.

claims.text: Non-GMO does not mean organic
claims.note: Avoiding excluded (genetic engineering) methods is only one of seven prohibitions in 7 CFR 205.105, beside synthetic substances, irradiation and sewage sludge, and organic also requires certification (205.100), so non-GMO alone does not meet the organic standard.

claims.text: Glyphosate residues are present in much of the conventional food supply
claims.note: Residue testing finds glyphosate commonly in grain, oat and soy foods, usually far below tolerances, but rarely on most fresh produce.

claims.text: Glyphosate is sprayed on wheat and other crops right before harvest as a drying agent
claims.note: Pre-harvest desiccation with glyphosate is a registered, documented practice on wheat, oats and pulses, though used on a minority of US wheat acres.

claims.text: Glyphosate in food drove the rise in celiac disease and gluten sensitivity
claims.note: Celiac disease is a genetic autoimmune condition; the glyphosate link rests on an ecological time-trend correlation, and rising celiac rates predate 2006.

claims.text: Glyphosate damages the human gut microbiome
claims.note: EFSA reviewed the published gut-microbiome studies and found no definitive conclusions can be drawn from them, while judging the mammalian toxicity dataset protective for any microbiome-mediated effect.

claims.text: Heavy glyphosate exposure raises the risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma
claims.note: EPA concluded glyphosate is not likely to be carcinogenic under real-world exposures, in line with EFSA, ECHA, Canada, Australia, Japan and JMPR, while noting IARC's hazard-based 2A rating answers a different question.

claims.text: Glyphosate use harms soil organisms
claims.note: Studies show some effects on soil microbes, fungi and earthworms, but many field studies find small or transient effects at label rates.

claims.text: Regulators approved glyphosate as safe because the agencies were captured by industry
claims.note: Many separate regulators (EFSA, ECHA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, FAO/WHO JMPR) reached EPA's conclusion, and EPA attributes the IARC split to hazard versus real-world risk scope; IARC (L219-221) notes regulators lean on unpublished industry data, which differs from capture.

claims.text: Pesticide drift from conventional farms contaminates organic crops
claims.note: Drift and volatilization of herbicides such as pendimethalin are documented, and residue surveys find low-level detections on some organic samples.

claims.text: Organic price premiums give sellers an incentive to pass off conventional food as organic
claims.note: Prosecuted fraud cases show sellers relabelling conventional grain and produce as organic to capture the premium.

claims.text: Organic eggs can carry more dioxin because hens forage outdoors
claims.note: Several European surveys found higher dioxin levels in free-range and organic eggs, usually still within legal limits.

claims.text: Organic farms may use manure compost from conventional animal operations, which can carry heavy metals
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.203(c) allows raw and composted animal manure without requiring it to come from organic animals, but requires managing it so it does not contaminate crops, soil or water with heavy metals; the rule shows the allowance and recognizes the heavy-metal risk, not how often contamination happens.

claims.text: Organic farming causes less ecotoxicity from pesticides than conventional farming
claims.note: Life-cycle meta-analyses find lower ecotoxicity for organic in nearly all comparisons, with copper-based fungicides the main exception.

claims.text: Organic and conventional farming have similar greenhouse gas emissions per kilogram of food
claims.note: Per unit of food, organic and conventional greenhouse gas emissions did not differ significantly (4% lower in organic, p=0.59, n=44), because manure N2O offsets savings from avoiding synthetic fertilizer; cradle-to-farm-gate, mostly industrialized systems.

claims.text: What you eat matters more for your food's carbon footprint than whether it is organic
claims.note: Differences between foods dwarf differences between production systems: ruminant meat has 20-100 times the impacts of plant foods on every indicator, whereas organic vs conventional differs by tens of percent and not at all on GHG.

claims.text: A global shift to organic farming could not feed the world without major diet changes
claims.note: Modelling studies find a fully organic system needs much more land and faces nitrogen shortfalls unless diets shift and food waste falls.

claims.text: Organic certifiers rarely test soil or produce for residues
claims.note: The required floor is low: under 7 CFR 205.670(d) certifiers need sample only 5 percent of operations a year, plus for-cause tests, so most operations need not be tested in a given year; the rule says nothing about how much testing certifiers do above that floor.

claims.text: Conventional grain sold as organic feed has reached organic meat, milk and eggs
claims.note: Prosecuted cases involved millions of bushels of conventional corn and soy sold as organic livestock feed.

claims.text: A significant share of food sold as organic is not genuinely organic
claims.note: Baden-Wuerttemberg's state lab judged 0% of fresh organic produce falsely labelled in 2021 (always well under 5% in 2011-2020, up to 8.5% before 2010) and 3.1% of processed organic foods (2.2-7.0% in recent years, over 8% before 2011); a German market and residue-based detection only, with targeted projects limiting year-to-year comparison.

claims.text: Group certification lets most farms in foreign organic grower groups go uninspected by accredited certifiers
claims.note: Under older rules certifiers inspected only a sample of group members and relied on internal control systems; the 2024 enforcement rule tightened this.

claims.text: Loosely checked organic imports undercut domestic organic farmers on price
claims.note: Cheap and sometimes fraudulent imports have depressed prices for some domestic organic grain and nut growers, though import competition has other causes too.

claims.text: Organic certification has conflicts of interest because farms choose and pay their own certifiers
claims.note: Operations do choose and pay accredited certifiers, a structural conflict, though USDA accredits and audits the certifiers.

claims.text: Hydroponic produce can be certified organic in the US
claims.note: USDA permits certification of hydroponic operations, a position upheld in federal court in 2022.

claims.text: Organic farming relies on more tillage, which can degrade soil
claims.note: Organic weed control often uses more tillage, which can harm soil structure, though organic systems still tend to have higher soil organic matter.

claims.text: Organic egg farms can meet outdoor-access rules with enclosed porches rather than pasture
claims.note: Porches have counted as outdoor access, but a 2023 USDA rule requires soil and vegetation outdoors, phased in by 2029 for existing farms.

claims.text: Eating organic is the only way to avoid harmful pesticide residues
claims.note: Probabilistic exposure modelling of the top ten pesticides on each Dirty Dozen crop put all 120 estimates below the chronic RfD (only one above 1%), so conventional residues were already negligible and organic produce is not residue-free either (23% positive).

claims.text: Hormones used in conventional beef and dairy raise cancer risk and cause early puberty
claims.note: Residues from approved beef implants and rbST are tiny next to natural hormone levels, and no causal link to cancer or early puberty is established.

claims.text: Buying organic is the most reliable way to avoid glyphosate in food
claims.note: Organic foods rarely carry glyphosate residues and diet switches lower urinary levels, though drift can leave traces and residue-tested labels also exist.

claims.text: Heavy glyphosate use has bred glyphosate-resistant superweeds
claims.note: Dozens of weed species have evolved glyphosate resistance, documented widely in Roundup Ready cropping systems.

claims.text: Pesticide residues on food act as estrogen mimics that drive hormonal cancers
claims.note: Some pesticides show endocrine activity in lab studies, but dietary residue levels have not been shown to cause breast or other hormonal cancers.

claims.text: Hormones are banned in all US poultry and pork, so a "no hormones" label on them adds nothing
claims.note: FSIS says hormones are not allowed in raising hogs or poultry, so 'no hormones added' on pork or poultry must carry the statement 'Federal regulations prohibit the use of hormones'.

claims.text: "No antibiotics" claims on meat require documentation submitted to USDA
claims.note: FSIS allows 'no antibiotics added' on meat or poultry only if the producer gives the agency enough documentation that the animals were raised without antibiotics.

claims.text: Pesticide risk is concentrated in a few conventional crops, so buying those organic cuts most of it
claims.note: Risk-weighted analyses of USDA residue data find a small set of crops, mostly with organophosphate or carbamate residues, account for most dietary pesticide risk.

claims.text: Organic certification inspections are often cursory
claims.note: Inspection depth varies by certifier and inspector, and there is no systematic measure of how thorough organic inspections are.

claims.text: The Strengthening Organic Enforcement rule closes supply-chain gaps that allowed organic fraud
claims.note: SOE covers several known gaps: it brings uncertified importers, traders and brokers under oversight, requires electronic import certificates for all organic imports, and adds traceability audits and fraud-prevention plans; this is the agency describing its own rule, with no data on whether fraud fell.

claims.text: Organic and conventional foods are equally likely to carry food-poisoning bacteria
claims.note: Systematic review (abstract only): E. coli risk did not differ for produce, and bacterial contamination of retail chicken and pork was common but unrelated to farming method.

claims.text: Organic food spoils faster than conventional food
claims.note: Few GM crops are engineered for shelf life, and studies find no consistent shelf-life difference attributable to organic production.

claims.text: Organic farming is more profitable for farmers than conventional farming
claims.note: A global meta-analysis found organic farms 22 to 35 percent more profitable when price premiums are paid, far below several-fold claims, and not without premiums.

claims.text: Healthy soil from organic farming produces healthier food and healthier people
claims.note: Soil health gains are measurable, but evidence linking organic soil management to better human health outcomes is lacking.

claims.text: Organic buyers are wealthier and healthier, which confounds studies of organic diets and health
claims.note: High organic consumers were more often female, higher-income, better educated, more active, leaner, and ate more fibre, fruit and vegetables and less meat, and the authors list residual confounding as a limitation.

claims.text: Organic rules bar modern crop varieties and efficient fertilizers
claims.note: The rules bar synthetic fertilizers not on the National List (205.203(e)) and genetically engineered varieties (205.105(e)), but they allow untreated conventional seed of any variety when no organic equivalent is available (205.204(a)), so modern conventionally bred varieties are not barred.

claims.text: Organic certification permits synthetic fertilizers
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.203(e)(1) bars any fertilizer containing a synthetic substance not on the National List; only listed synthetics such as micronutrients for documented deficiencies and pH-adjusted fish products are allowed (205.601(j)), so general synthetic fertilizers such as synthetic nitrogen are not permitted.

claims.text: Post-harvest coatings that extend shelf life are allowed on organic produce
claims.note: At least one plant-lipid shelf-life coating has an organic-approved formulation, and coatings from allowed substances can be used on organic produce.

claims.text: A grass-fed label does not guarantee the animal was raised on pasture
claims.note: Generic grass-fed claims describe diet and are approved company by company; only some third-party certifiers also require pasture.

claims.text: Most grass-fed beef sold in the US is imported
claims.note: Industry analyses have estimated that most US grass-fed beef at retail comes from Australia, New Zealand and South America.

claims.text: The organic label describes farming practices rather than health or nutrition benefits
claims.note: The organic label certifies approved production and handling methods; ERS notes the USDA organic regulations do not address the health and safety of organic foods.

claims.text: Virtually no US retail milk comes from rBST-treated cows, so rBST-free labels add nothing
claims.note: Use of rBST has fallen to a small minority of herds and most processors refuse it, but it is still approved and not entirely gone.

claims.text: Non-GMO labels often appear on foods that have no genetically engineered version
claims.note: Only a handful of crops have commercial GE varieties, yet non-GMO claims appear on many products that could never be genetically engineered.

claims.text: Genetically engineered crops are nutritionally equivalent to their conventional counterparts
claims.note: Compositional studies reviewed by the National Academies found approved GE crops nutritionally equivalent to conventional ones, apart from deliberately altered traits.

claims.text: Routine residue testing does not check for most pesticides used in organic farming
claims.note: The Pesticide Data Program tests hundreds of compounds including some used in organic, but it does not measure substances such as copper and sulfur.

claims.text: Natural pesticides approved for organic use are less thoroughly safety-tested than synthetic ones
claims.note: Some older natural pesticides were grandfathered with thinner data packages, but EPA still has to register them and many are low-risk biopesticides.

claims.text: Organic produce may legally carry synthetic pesticide residues up to a small fraction of the legal tolerance
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.671 excludes a product from organic sale only when residue testing finds prohibited substances above 5 percent of the EPA tolerance, so residues below that fraction do not by themselves cost the organic label.

claims.text: Milk from pasture-fed cows has more omega-3 fatty acids than milk from grain-fed cows
claims.note: In the cross-European survey, grazing intake was strongly positively associated with milk PUFA, n-3 PUFA, ALA and CLA, while concentrate and silage intakes were negatively associated.

claims.text: Some large certified organic dairies have violated pasture requirements
claims.note: The USDA has cited large organic dairies for pasture violations, and investigative reporting has found big herds with little grazing.

claims.text: Ultra-pasteurization strips milk of much of its nutritional value
claims.note: UHT causes modest losses of some heat-sensitive vitamins but leaves protein, calcium and most nutrients largely intact.

claims.text: Some sellers have passed off conventional food as organic
claims.note: The state lab judged 3.1% of processed organic foods falsely labelled as organic in 2021 (2.2-7.0% in recent years, over 8% before 2011), naming each case: chives, US almonds, Chinese goji berries, Turkish figs and Ghanaian pineapple carrying prohibited herbicides or insecticides.

claims.text: Pesticide safety limits do not account for long-term daily exposure
claims.note: The EPA chronic RfD used as the benchmark is defined as the daily amount a person could take in throughout their lifetime without appreciable risk, so safety limits are built on long-term daily exposure.

claims.text: Organic crops carry a higher risk of mycotoxin contamination
claims.note: Reviews of organic and conventional cereals find similar or lower mycotoxin levels in organic grain.

claims.text: Organic chickens live in the same indoor conditions as conventional chickens, differing only in feed
claims.note: Organic poultry rules go beyond feed: 7 CFR 205.238 requires conditions for exercise and freedom of movement and bans de-beaking and induced molting; the excerpt omits the avian outdoor-access rules, so it does not show how indoor conditions actually differ.

claims.text: Pasture-raised eggs are more nutritious than conventional eggs
claims.note: Pastured hens' eggs tend to have more omega-3, vitamin E and carotenoids, but the size of the difference varies and it is modest for overall nutrition.

claims.text: A grass-fed label does not guarantee the animal was grass-finished
claims.note: Without a 100 percent grass-fed or grass-finished claim or certification, cattle labelled grass-fed may have been finished on grain.

claims.text: Modern crops contain far fewer vitamins and minerals than crops grown decades ago
claims.note: Historical comparisons show modest declines in some minerals, mostly from high-yield varieties, nowhere near several-fold losses.

claims.text: Organic meat has similar or higher greenhouse gas emissions than conventional meat
claims.note: Life-cycle studies generally find organic meat's emissions per kilogram similar to or above conventional meat because of slower growth and more land use.

claims.text: Organic plant foods have lower greenhouse gas emissions than conventional plant foods
claims.note: Skipping synthetic nitrogen cuts emissions, but per-kilogram comparisons are mixed once lower yields and extra land are counted.

claims.text: Grass-fed cattle emit more methane per kilogram of beef than grain-fed cattle
claims.note: Grass-finished cattle grow more slowly and produce more enteric methane per kilogram of beef, though soil carbon may offset part of it.

claims.text: Organic rules exclude some practices that would make food safer or more sustainable
claims.note: Organic rules ban irradiation, biosolids and GE crops, which have food-safety or environmental benefits in some uses, though each has trade-offs.

claims.text: Some pesticides used in conventional farming disrupt hormones at dietary exposure levels
claims.note: Several pesticides are endocrine disruptors at higher doses, but harm at typical dietary residue levels has not been shown.

claims.text: Genetically engineered foods carry long-term health risks
claims.note: Major scientific reviews find no evidence that approved GE foods pose greater health risks than conventional foods.

claims.text: Organic product labels must be approved by an accredited certifier before use
claims.note: Under the NOP rules, certifiers review and approve organic labels as part of certification.

claims.text: Real Organic Project certification adds requirements beyond USDA Organic, such as banning hydroponics and animal confinement
claims.note: Real Organic Project is an add-on to USDA Organic that requires soil-grown crops and pasture-based livestock.

claims.text: Pasture-raised egg labels mean hens spend most of the day outdoors with ample space
claims.note: There is no USDA definition of pasture-raised; only third-party certifications such as Certified Humane set outdoor space and time rules.

claims.text: Organic farming stores more carbon in soil than conventional farming
claims.note: Organic soils often hold more carbon, but much of it comes from imported manure, and the net sequestration gain is debated.

claims.text: Fat-soluble pesticides and pollutants in the diet come mostly from animal foods
claims.note: Persistent organochlorines, dioxins and PCBs build up in animal fat, and most dietary exposure comes from meat, dairy and fish.

claims.text: Heavy occupational pesticide exposure is linked to higher cancer risk
claims.note: Studies of applicators and farm workers link high exposure to some pesticides with cancers such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

claims.text: The National List generally allows natural substances and prohibits synthetic ones, with exceptions
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.105 bars synthetic substances except those listed in 205.601/603 and bars nonsynthetic substances only where 205.602/604 prohibit them (e.g. arsenic, strychnine, rotenone), so natural is allowed and synthetic prohibited by default, with listed exceptions both ways.

claims.text: Certified organic farms must use organic seeds when available
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.204(a) requires organically grown seed and planting stock, but allows untreated nonorganic seed when an equivalent organic variety is not commercially available (never for edible sprouts).

claims.text: Organic meat carries about the same load of carcinogenic pollutants as conventional meat
claims.note: A Spanish study found minimal differences in persistent pollutants between organic and conventional meat, but the evidence comes from very few studies.

claims.text: Organic livestock must be fed organic feed
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.237(a) requires a total feed ration of certified organic agricultural products, pasture and forage included, with allowed synthetic additives and supplements and narrow exceptions for transitioning dairy and breeder stock.

claims.text: Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer leads crops to make fewer defensive phytonutrients
claims.note: Higher nitrogen availability is linked to lower phenolic content in some crops, but the effect varies and is not the only cause.

claims.text: Organic operations are subject to unannounced inspections and residue testing
claims.note: The SOE final rule requires certifiers to make unannounced inspections of at least 5 percent of the operations they certify, along with mass-balance audits at annual on-site inspections.

claims.text: USDA traceability rules make organic fraud harder by tracking products back to the farm
claims.note: The 2024 Strengthening Organic Enforcement rule added import certificates and supply-chain audits, but how much fraud it prevents is not yet measured.

claims.text: Organic food can still contain glyphosate residues
claims.note: The 5-percent-of-tolerance exclusion in 7 CFR 205.671 means organic food may legally carry trace residues of prohibited pesticides such as glyphosate; the rule shows this is allowed, not how often it occurs.

claims.text: Herbicide-tolerant GM crops are sprayed with glyphosate, leaving residues in the food
claims.note: Glyphosate-tolerant crops are sprayed and can carry residues, though highly refined products such as oils and sugar contain little.

claims.text: A PLU code beginning with 9 identifies organic produce
claims.note: Under the IFPS convention, a 9 prefix on a four-digit PLU marks organic produce, though use is voluntary.

claims.text: A PLU code beginning with 8 identifies genetically engineered produce
claims.note: The 8 prefix was never adopted for GE produce, and IFPS has since dropped it and reassigns 8-series codes to new items.

claims.text: US law does not require genetically engineered foods to be labelled
claims.note: Since 2022 the National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard has required disclosure of bioengineered foods, though with exemptions.

claims.text: The FDA's informal natural policy only means nothing artificial or synthetic was added
claims.note: FDA's longstanding policy is that 'natural' means nothing artificial or synthetic, color additives included, was added that would not normally be in the food; it was not meant to cover production methods such as pesticides, processing methods, or health benefits.

claims.text: High pesticide exposure is linked to Parkinson's disease
claims.note: Meta-analyses of occupational and rural cohorts show raised Parkinson's risk with pesticide exposure, notably paraquat.

claims.text: Prenatal organophosphate pesticide exposure is linked to lower IQ and neurodevelopmental problems in children
claims.note: US birth cohorts (CHAMACOS, two New York cohorts) link maternal organophosphate or cord-blood chlorpyrifos levels to poorer mental development, attention problems and lower IQ at 7, and reviews conclude general-population prenatal exposure likely harms neurodevelopment; a French cohort with lower exposure did not replicate.

claims.text: Herbicide-tolerant GM crops increase herbicide use
claims.note: Herbicide-tolerant crops raised glyphosate use and drove resistant weeds, while Bt crops cut insecticide use.

claims.text: Agricultural pesticides harm biodiversity, water quality and soil
claims.note: Pesticides are a documented driver of insect and aquatic biodiversity loss and of water contamination.

claims.text: The US permits many pesticides that the EU has banned
claims.note: Comparative studies show dozens of pesticides approved in the US are banned or unapproved in the EU.

claims.text: Organic farming cannot feed the world's current population
claims.note: About half of food output depends on synthetic nitrogen; models suggest an organic world is feasible only with large cuts in waste and animal feed.

claims.text: Abruptly banning synthetic fertilizer sharply cuts crop yields
claims.note: Sri Lanka's 2021 fertilizer ban was followed by steep rice and tea output falls and was reversed within months.

claims.text: Plants cannot tell synthetic nitrogen from organic nitrogen
claims.note: Plants take up mineral nitrate and ammonium whatever the source, though organic inputs also change soil structure and release timing.

claims.text: Grain-fed beef harms health in ways grass-fed beef does not
claims.note: No outcome studies show grass-fed beef eaters fare better; fat-profile differences are small relative to total diet.

claims.text: Several of the most commonly detected pesticide residues on produce are PFAS chemicals
claims.note: Fludioxonil, fluopyram and bifenthrin carry fluorinated groups meeting the OECD PFAS definition, though their risk differs from legacy PFAS.

claims.text: Organic farming requires more labour than conventional farming
claims.note: Weeding and pest control without herbicides raise labour per hectare on most organic farms.

claims.text: Pesticide residues in food cause large numbers of deaths worldwide
claims.note: The UN figure refers to acute pesticide poisonings, mostly occupational exposure and self-harm, not residues in food.

claims.text: Most conventional grain crops are sprayed with glyphosate before harvest
claims.note: Pre-harvest desiccation is used on a minority of US wheat and on oats mainly in Canada, not on most corn or soy.

claims.text: Taking glycine supplements protects the body from glyphosate
claims.note: There is no human evidence that supplemental glycine blocks glyphosate uptake or effects.

claims.text: The extra omega-3 and CLA in grass-fed dairy meaningfully improve consumer health
claims.note: Even grass-fed milk supplies little omega-3 next to fish, and no trials show health outcomes from these differences.

claims.text: Organic eggs carry fewer pesticide residues because the hens eat organic feed
claims.note: Organic feed lowers pesticide inputs, but residues in conventional eggs are already rare and very low.

claims.text: Growing your own vegetables improves physical and mental health
claims.note: Gardening studies show modest gains in activity and wellbeing, mostly from observational and small trials.

claims.text: Genetically engineered crops are as safe to eat as conventionally bred crops
claims.note: The 2016 National Academies review found no evidence that approved engineered crops are less safe to eat.

claims.text: Organic farmland in France shrank after 2022 as farmers dropped certification
claims.note: French Agence Bio data show certified organic area fell from 2022 to 2024 as some farms deconverted.

claims.text: Organic farmers are more exposed to price shocks than conventional farmers
claims.note: Organic premiums collapsed with inflation in 2022-23, though organic farms also receive specific EU subsidies.

claims.text: An organic label leads people to underestimate a food's calories
claims.note: Experiments on the organic halo show people rate organic-labelled snacks as lower in calories.

claims.text: Conventional livestock are fed sewage sludge
claims.note: Biosolids are spread on some cropland and pasture under EPA rules, but they are not fed to livestock as feed.

claims.text: Products with under 70 percent organic content can only name organic ingredients in the ingredient list
claims.note: 7 CFR 205.301(d) says products with under 70 percent organic ingredients may represent their organic nature only as 205.305 provides; 205.305 (identifying organic ingredients in the ingredient statement) is not in this excerpt.

commonlyWrong.text: The Dirty Dozen list is a reliable guide to which produce to buy organic
commonlyWrong.note: The 2010 EWG method ignored food consumption and toxicological thresholds and was skewed toward counts of multiple residues, so it could not rank risk (blueberries, cherries and kale had all exposures over 30,000-fold below RfDs); EWG has since added a toxicity factor but still no consumption weighting.

commonlyWrong.text: Organic labelling is mainly a marketing tool to charge higher prices
commonlyWrong.note: The organic label is a legally enforced production standard with inspections and real input restrictions, even though it is heavily marketed.

commonlyWrong.text: Glyphosate residues in food harm human health
commonlyWrong.note: EFSA's 2023 peer review put the maximum chronic dietary intake of glyphosate at 3% of the ADI (Dutch toddlers) and acute intake at 2% of the ARfD; provisional, limited to the EU's representative uses, but an independent regulator finding dietary residues far below levels of concern.

commonlyWrong.text: Eating organic food has proven health benefits for the people who eat it
commonlyWrong.note: The review concludes the link between organic food and health is insufficiently documented and that it is not possible to tell whether organic food plays a causal role in observed lower allergy, obesity or NHL, given residual confounding.

commonlyWrong.text: Regulators assess pesticides one at a time and ignore combined effects of residue mixtures
commonlyWrong.note: EFSA ran a cumulative risk assessment of dietary residues, adding doses across pesticides with a common effect and computing a combined margin of exposure at each percentile, so EU regulators do assess combined effects within effect groups.

commonlyWrong.text: A significant share of food sold as organic is not genuinely organic
commonlyWrong.note: Baden-Wuerttemberg's state lab judged 0% of fresh organic produce falsely labelled in 2021 (always well under 5% in 2011-2020, up to 8.5% before 2010) and 3.1% of processed organic foods (2.2-7.0% in recent years, over 8% before 2011); a German market and residue-based detection only, with targeted projects limiting year-to-year comparison.

commonlyWrong.text: Eating organic food lowers cancer risk
commonlyWrong.note: In 623,080 UK women followed 9.3 years (53,769 cancers), usually/always eating organic food was not linked to lower total cancer (RR 1.03, 0.99-1.07; 1.00 among consistent consumers), breast cancer was slightly higher (RR 1.09), and only NHL was lower (RR 0.79), which the authors say may be chance.

commonlyWrong.text: Organic farming uses no pesticides
commonlyWrong.note: 7 CFR 205.206(e) lets organic producers apply biological or botanical substances or National List synthetics to control pests, weeds and diseases when cultural, mechanical and physical methods are not enough, so organic farming does use pesticides.

commonlyWrong.text: Organic farming bans all synthetic pesticides
commonlyWrong.note: Annex I of EU Regulation 2021/1165 authorises plant protection active substances for organic production including paraffin oils, lime sulphur, copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, Bordeaux mixture and the synthetic pyrethroids deltamethrin and lambda-cyhalothrin (in traps only), so EU organic rules do not ban all synthetic pesticides.

commonlyWrong.text: Heavy glyphosate exposure raises the risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma
commonlyWrong.note: EPA concluded glyphosate is not likely to be carcinogenic under real-world exposures, in line with EFSA, ECHA, Canada, Australia, Japan and JMPR, while noting IARC's hazard-based 2A rating answers a different question.

commonlyWrong.text: Organic food tastes better than conventional food
commonlyWrong.note: Blind taste tests show no consistent preference for organic; label-aware tests show a halo effect.

commonlyWrong.text: Genetically engineered foods carry long-term health risks
commonlyWrong.note: Major scientific reviews find no evidence that approved GE foods pose greater health risks than conventional foods.

commonlyWrong.text: Organic produce carries a higher risk of bacterial contamination than conventional produce
commonlyWrong.note: The Stanford meta-analysis found no significant difference in E. coli contamination between organic and conventional produce.

commonlyWrong.text: Conventional livestock are fed sewage sludge
commonlyWrong.note: Biosolids are spread on some cropland and pasture under EPA rules, but they are not fed to livestock as feed.

commonlyWrong.text: Eating organic is the only way to avoid harmful pesticide residues
commonlyWrong.note: Probabilistic exposure modelling of the top ten pesticides on each Dirty Dozen crop put all 120 estimates below the chronic RfD (only one above 1%), so conventional residues were already negligible and organic produce is not residue-free either (23% positive).

commonlyWrong.text: The extra omega-3 and CLA in grass-fed dairy meaningfully improve consumer health
commonlyWrong.note: Even grass-fed milk supplies little omega-3 next to fish, and no trials show health outcomes from these differences.

commonlyWrong.text: Glyphosate in food drove the rise in celiac disease and gluten sensitivity
commonlyWrong.note: Celiac disease is a genetic autoimmune condition; the glyphosate link rests on an ecological time-trend correlation, and rising celiac rates predate 2006.

commonlyWrong.text: Grain-fed beef harms health in ways grass-fed beef does not
commonlyWrong.note: No outcome studies show grass-fed beef eaters fare better; fat-profile differences are small relative to total diet.

commonlyWrong.text: Hormones used in conventional beef and dairy raise cancer risk and cause early puberty
commonlyWrong.note: Residues from approved beef implants and rbST are tiny next to natural hormone levels, and no causal link to cancer or early puberty is established.

commonlyWrong.text: US law does not require genetically engineered foods to be labelled
commonlyWrong.note: Since 2022 the National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard has required disclosure of bioengineered foods, though with exemptions.

commonlyWrong.text: Modern crops contain far fewer vitamins and minerals than crops grown decades ago
commonlyWrong.note: Historical comparisons show modest declines in some minerals, mostly from high-yield varieties, nowhere near several-fold losses.

commonlyWrong.text: Most conventional grain crops are sprayed with glyphosate before harvest
commonlyWrong.note: Pre-harvest desiccation is used on a minority of US wheat and on oats mainly in Canada, not on most corn or soy.

commonlyWrong.text: Organic certification permits synthetic fertilizers
commonlyWrong.note: 7 CFR 205.203(e)(1) bars any fertilizer containing a synthetic substance not on the National List; only listed synthetics such as micronutrients for documented deficiencies and pH-adjusted fish products are allowed (205.601(j)), so general synthetic fertilizers such as synthetic nitrogen are not permitted.

commonlyWrong.text: Organic certification sets no living-condition rules for laying hens
commonlyWrong.note: 7 CFR 205.238 applies to all organic livestock, poultry included: it requires housing that limits disease and conditions allowing exercise, freedom of movement and lower stress, and it bans de-beaking, beak trimming after 10 days and induced molting (the avian living-conditions section 205.241 is not in this excerpt).

commonlyWrong.text: Organic chickens live in the same indoor conditions as conventional chickens, differing only in feed
commonlyWrong.note: Organic poultry rules go beyond feed: 7 CFR 205.238 requires conditions for exercise and freedom of movement and bans de-beaking and induced molting; the excerpt omits the avian outdoor-access rules, so it does not show how indoor conditions actually differ.

commonlyWrong.text: Organic crops carry a higher risk of mycotoxin contamination
commonlyWrong.note: Reviews of organic and conventional cereals find similar or lower mycotoxin levels in organic grain.

commonlyWrong.text: Organic food spoils faster than conventional food
commonlyWrong.note: Few GM crops are engineered for shelf life, and studies find no consistent shelf-life difference attributable to organic production.

commonlyWrong.text: Pesticide residues on food act as estrogen mimics that drive hormonal cancers
commonlyWrong.note: Some pesticides show endocrine activity in lab studies, but dietary residue levels have not been shown to cause breast or other hormonal cancers.

commonlyWrong.text: Pesticide residues in food cause large numbers of deaths worldwide
commonlyWrong.note: The UN figure refers to acute pesticide poisonings, mostly occupational exposure and self-harm, not residues in food.

commonlyWrong.text: Pesticide safety limits do not account for long-term daily exposure
commonlyWrong.note: The EPA chronic RfD used as the benchmark is defined as the daily amount a person could take in throughout their lifetime without appreciable risk, so safety limits are built on long-term daily exposure.

commonlyWrong.text: A PLU code beginning with 8 identifies genetically engineered produce
commonlyWrong.note: The 8 prefix was never adopted for GE produce, and IFPS has since dropped it and reassigns 8-series codes to new items.

commonlyWrong.text: Regenerative organic farming yields far more than industrial agriculture
commonlyWrong.note: Even with diversification practices (organic polycultures or more rotations) the organic yield gap shrank to 9% and 8% but did not reverse; no setting showed organic yielding far more than conventional.

commonlyWrong.text: Regulators approved glyphosate as safe because the agencies were captured by industry
commonlyWrong.note: Many separate regulators (EFSA, ECHA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, FAO/WHO JMPR) reached EPA's conclusion, and EPA attributes the IARC split to hazard versus real-world risk scope; IARC (L219-221) notes regulators lean on unpublished industry data, which differs from capture.

commonlyWrong.text: Ultra-pasteurization strips milk of much of its nutritional value
commonlyWrong.note: UHT causes modest losses of some heat-sensitive vitamins but leaves protein, calcium and most nutrients largely intact.

claim.text: Regulators assess pesticides one at a time and ignore combined effects of residue mixtures
claim.note: EFSA ran a cumulative risk assessment of dietary residues, adding doses across pesticides with a common effect and computing a combined margin of exposure at each percentile, so EU regulators do assess combined effects within effect groups.

priorRecord.note: Approvals are mostly per active substance; EFSA and EPA run cumulative assessments for some chemical groups, but mixture effects remain little studied.

evidenceRecord.note: EFSA ran a cumulative risk assessment of dietary residues, adding doses across pesticides with a common effect and computing a combined margin of exposure at each percentile, so EU regulators do assess combined effects within effect groups.

claim.text: Organic standards require higher animal welfare than conventional farming
claim.note: 7 CFR 205.238-205.239 set welfare rules, among them year-round outdoor access, no continuous total confinement, bans on gestation and farrowing crates, de-beaking and induced molting, and conditions allowing freedom of movement; the regulation does not itself compare these with conventional practice or say how they are enforced.

priorRecord.note: Organic rules mandate outdoor access, pasture for ruminants and bans on some confinement practices, though they are weaker than dedicated welfare certifications.

claim.text: Pesticide residues on conventional produce are too low to harm health
claim.note: For the ten most detected pesticides on each 2010 Dirty Dozen crop, RfDs exceeded mean exposure in every case and by over 1000-fold in more than 90% of comparisons; limited to 2004-2008 data, top-ten pesticides and mean (not high-end) exposure.

priorRecord.note: USDA testing finds nearly all samples below EPA tolerances and no clear harm is shown, but chronic low-dose and mixture effects are not well studied.

priorRecord.note: It ranks produce by residue detections, which helps cut residue exposure, but ignores dose and toxicity relative to safety limits.

claim.text: Pesticides allowed in organic farming are not necessarily safer than synthetic ones
claim.note: Most EU organic-approved pesticides are of low concern (none classed as suspected carcinogens or reproductive toxicants vs 27 and 26 among all approved), but pyrethrins share the pyrethroid mechanism and copper is toxic at high intake and ecotoxic, so some are not safer.

priorRecord.note: Organic reliably lowers residue exposure, but no health outcome benefit has been shown to justify the premium on health grounds alone.

evidenceRecord.note: On the pesticide rationale alone, substituting organic for conventional Dirty Dozen produce showed no measurable consumer health benefit because conventional exposures were negligible; nutrition and other reasons not assessed.

claim.text: Grass-fed beef has a healthier fat profile than grain-fed beef
claim.note: Cited controlled experiment: switching beef from grain to grass finishing raised intramuscular PUFA 45%, n-3 PUFA over 3-fold, EPA over 5-fold and DHA 129%, with no change in n-6; forage diets also lower SFA in meat.

priorRecord.note: Grass-fed beef has more omega-3 and CLA and a better omega ratio, but the absolute amounts are small for health.

claim.text: Organic meat carries fewer antibiotic-resistant bacteria than conventional meat
claim.note: Organic pork and chicken are less likely to harbour resistant bacteria, resistance is less common in organic pigs in four countries, and converting poultry farms to organic cut resistant Salmonella; MRSA differences lost significance after adjustment.

claim.text: Imported organic products must meet the same standards as domestic organic products
claim.note: Imports may be certified under foreign equivalency arrangements that need only be 'at least equivalent', not identical; OIG found 25 procedural and 9 technical differences in one arrangement and 68 and 28 in another, with no documented resolution of all of them.

claim.note: Studies show some effects on soil microbes, fungi and earthworms, but many field studies find small or transient effects at label rates.
