priorRecord.note: Grass-finished cattle grow more slowly and produce more enteric methane per kilogram of beef, though soil carbon may offset part of it.

evidenceRecord.note: In 7 paired systems grass-fed beef had 19% higher GHG per unit food (not significant, p=0.22), which the authors attribute to slower growth and slaughter 6-12 months later raising lifetime methane; the direction fits, but the sample is small and the difference not significant.

claim.text: Heavy occupational pesticide exposure is linked to higher cancer risk
claim.note: Studies of applicators and farm workers link high exposure to some pesticides with cancers such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

priorRecord.note: Studies of applicators and farm workers link high exposure to some pesticides with cancers such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

evidenceRecord.note: For one pesticide, glyphosate, occupational studies across regions and formulations reported similar increases in non-Hodgkin lymphoma, backed by animal and genotoxicity data; IARC still rates the human evidence 'limited'.

claim.text: Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer leads crops to make fewer defensive phytonutrients
claim.note: Higher nitrogen availability is linked to lower phenolic content in some crops, but the effect varies and is not the only cause.

priorRecord.note: Higher nitrogen availability is linked to lower phenolic content in some crops, but the effect varies and is not the only cause.

evidenceRecord.note: Authors cite increasing evidence that high mineral N inputs lower phenolic defence compounds (wheat, apple, tomato), with plants shifting carbon to growth under high N, but say more research is needed to separate fertiliser from pest effects.

claim.text: Agricultural pesticides harm biodiversity, water quality and soil
claim.note: Pesticides are a documented driver of insect and aquatic biodiversity loss and of water contamination.

priorRecord.note: Pesticides are a documented driver of insect and aquatic biodiversity loss and of water contamination.

evidenceRecord.note: For glyphosate, EPA found ecological risks to non-target plants, mammals and birds and judged it 'likely to adversely affect' 93% of listed species and 96% of critical habitats; biodiversity harm is supported for this herbicide, water and soil harm are not shown here.

claim.text: The US permits many pesticides that the EU has banned
claim.note: Comparative studies show dozens of pesticides approved in the US are banned or unapproved in the EU.

priorRecord.note: Comparative studies show dozens of pesticides approved in the US are banned or unapproved in the EU.

evidenceRecord.note: One documented example: chlorpropham, found on 90% of US potatoes, lost EU approval in 2019; a single case supports the pattern but not the 'many'.

contested.text: Organic food costs substantially more than conventional food
contested.note: Hedonic model on 2004-10 Nielsen Homescan purchases, controlling for package, brand, store and market, found positive organic premiums for all 17 products, above 20% for 16 of them (2010: 7% spinach to 82% eggs); meat and poultry were not covered.

contested.text: Pesticide residues on conventional produce are too low to harm health
contested.note: For the ten most detected pesticides on each 2010 Dirty Dozen crop, RfDs exceeded mean exposure in every case and by over 1000-fold in more than 90% of comparisons; limited to 2004-2008 data, top-ten pesticides and mean (not high-end) exposure.

contested.text: The Dirty Dozen list is a reliable guide to which produce to buy organic
contested.note: The 2010 EWG method ignored food consumption and toxicological thresholds and was skewed toward counts of multiple residues, so it could not rank risk (blueberries, cherries and kale had all exposures over 30,000-fold below RfDs); EWG has since added a toxicity factor but still no consumption weighting.

contested.text: Pesticides allowed in organic farming are not necessarily safer than synthetic ones
contested.note: Most EU organic-approved pesticides are of low concern (none classed as suspected carcinogens or reproductive toxicants vs 27 and 26 among all approved), but pyrethrins share the pyrethroid mechanism and copper is toxic at high intake and ecotoxic, so some are not safer.

contested.text: Organic farming is better for the environment than conventional farming
contested.note: Per unit of food, organic used 15% less energy but needed 25-110% more land and had 37% higher eutrophication, with similar GHG and acidification; the authors say this does not make conventional more sustainable given its pesticide and nutrient inputs, which they could not measure.

contested.text: Organic farming yields less food per acre than conventional farming
contested.note: Hierarchical meta-analysis of 115 studies (1071 comparisons, 38 countries) found organic yields 19.2% lower (95% CI 15.5-22.9%), with conventional higher for all crop types; the authors note publication bias may overstate the gap.

contested.text: Imported organic food is less trustworthy than domestic organic food
contested.note: The largest documented organic fraud cases involved imported grain, though imports must meet the same rules and enforcement tightened under the 2023 SOE rule.

contested.text: Organic milk and meat contain more omega-3 fatty acids than conventional milk and meat
contested.note: Meta-analysis of 170 studies on cow's milk: weighted analysis found total n-3 PUFA 56% higher in organic milk (ALA +68%, EPA +67%, DPA +45%), GRADE moderate, robust across sensitivity analyses.

contested.text: The "natural" label has little regulatory meaning
contested.note: FDA has never formally defined 'natural' and has only an informal policy (nothing artificial or synthetic added) that does not address pesticides, processing or health; FSIS's meat definition (no artificial ingredients, minimally processed) likewise says nothing about how the animal was raised.

contested.text: Organic farming improves soil health
contested.note: Long-term trials show higher soil organic matter and biological activity under organic management, partly from manure and compost inputs.

contested.text: Organic labelling is mainly a marketing tool to charge higher prices
contested.note: The organic label is a legally enforced production standard with inspections and real input restrictions, even though it is heavily marketed.

contested.text: Organic certification requires grazing animals to have access to pasture
contested.note: 7 CFR 205.237(c) requires ruminants to graze through the whole grazing season, at least 120 days a year, and to get on average at least 30 percent of their dry matter intake from pasture.

contested.text: Organic food is more nutritious than conventional food
contested.note: Crop vitamins and minerals are similar under both systems; organic has modestly more phenolics and its dairy about 50% more omega-3, but the review calls established nutritional differences small with no strong health conclusions.

contested.text: Eating organic food has proven health benefits for the people who eat it
contested.note: The review concludes the link between organic food and health is insufficiently documented and that it is not possible to tell whether organic food plays a causal role in observed lower allergy, obesity or NHL, given residual confounding.

contested.text: A significant share of food sold as organic is not genuinely organic
contested.note: Baden-Wuerttemberg's state lab judged 0% of fresh organic produce falsely labelled in 2021 (always well under 5% in 2011-2020, up to 8.5% before 2010) and 3.1% of processed organic foods (2.2-7.0% in recent years, over 8% before 2011); a German market and residue-based detection only, with targeted projects limiting year-to-year comparison.

contested.text: Organic food is worth its price premium for health reasons
contested.note: Organic reliably lowers residue exposure, but no health outcome benefit has been shown to justify the premium on health grounds alone.

contested.text: Eating organic food lowers cancer risk
contested.note: In 623,080 UK women followed 9.3 years (53,769 cancers), usually/always eating organic food was not linked to lower total cancer (RR 1.03, 0.99-1.07; 1.00 among consistent consumers), breast cancer was slightly higher (RR 1.09), and only NHL was lower (RR 0.79), which the authors say may be chance.

contested.text: Organic farming uses no pesticides
contested.note: 7 CFR 205.206(e) lets organic producers apply biological or botanical substances or National List synthetics to control pests, weeds and diseases when cultural, mechanical and physical methods are not enough, so organic farming does use pesticides.

contested.text: Grass-fed beef has a healthier fat profile than grain-fed beef
contested.note: Cited controlled experiment: switching beef from grain to grass finishing raised intramuscular PUFA 45%, n-3 PUFA over 3-fold, EPA over 5-fold and DHA 129%, with no change in n-6; forage diets also lower SFA in meat.

contested.text: Organic farming bans all synthetic pesticides
contested.note: Annex I of EU Regulation 2021/1165 authorises plant protection active substances for organic production including paraffin oils, lime sulphur, copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, Bordeaux mixture and the synthetic pyrethroids deltamethrin and lambda-cyhalothrin (in traps only), so EU organic rules do not ban all synthetic pesticides.

contested.text: Washing produce removes most pesticide residue
contested.note: Rinsing and baking-soda soaks remove part of surface residues, but systemic and absorbed residues stay in the produce.

contested.text: Organic and conventional foods are equally likely to carry food-poisoning bacteria
contested.note: Systematic review (abstract only): E. coli risk did not differ for produce, and bacterial contamination of retail chicken and pork was common but unrelated to farming method.

contested.text: Organic food tastes better than conventional food
contested.note: Blind taste tests show no consistent preference for organic; label-aware tests show a halo effect.

contested.text: A global shift to organic farming could not feed the world without major diet changes
contested.note: Modelling studies find a fully organic system needs much more land and faces nitrogen shortfalls unless diets shift and food waste falls.

contested.text: Organic standards require higher animal welfare than conventional farming
contested.note: 7 CFR 205.238-205.239 set welfare rules, among them year-round outdoor access, no continuous total confinement, bans on gestation and farrowing crates, de-beaking and induced molting, and conditions allowing freedom of movement; the regulation does not itself compare these with conventional practice or say how they are enforced.

thinEvidence.text: Cage-free and free-range labels say little about how hens actually live
thinEvidence.note: USDA free-range requires only some outdoor access and cage-free only no cages, with no space, duration or outdoor-quality minimums.

thinEvidence.text: Organic processed foods are no healthier than their conventional counterparts
thinEvidence.note: Organic snacks and cereals have similar sugar, fat and calories to conventional versions; the seal certifies ingredients' farming, not the product's nutrition.

thinEvidence.text: Regenerative Organic Certified sets stricter standards than USDA Organic for soil, animal welfare and labour
thinEvidence.note: ROC requires USDA Organic as a baseline and adds soil-health, animal-welfare and farmworker-fairness requirements.

thinEvidence.text: Small farms can be organic in practice without being certified
thinEvidence.note: Certification costs and paperwork lead some small growers to farm organically uncertified; operations under 5,000 dollars in sales are exempt.

thinEvidence.text: Much organic meat and dairy comes from large industrial-scale operations
thinEvidence.note: A large share of US organic milk and eggs comes from operations with thousands of animals, though they must meet pasture and outdoor rules.

thinEvidence.text: Conventional grain sold as organic feed has reached organic meat, milk and eggs
thinEvidence.note: Prosecuted cases involved millions of bushels of conventional corn and soy sold as organic livestock feed.

thinEvidence.text: Fear of pesticide residues discourages people from eating fruit and vegetables
thinEvidence.note: One survey experiment found low-income shoppers less willing to buy produce after residue messaging; real-world effects are unmeasured.

thinEvidence.text: Hydroponic produce can be certified organic in the US
thinEvidence.note: USDA permits certification of hydroponic operations, a position upheld in federal court in 2022.

thinEvidence.text: Glyphosate is sprayed on wheat and other crops right before harvest as a drying agent
thinEvidence.note: Pre-harvest desiccation with glyphosate is a registered, documented practice on wheat, oats and pulses, though used on a minority of US wheat acres.

thinEvidence.text: A grass-fed label does not guarantee the animal was grass-finished
thinEvidence.note: Without a 100 percent grass-fed or grass-finished claim or certification, cattle labelled grass-fed may have been finished on grain.

thinEvidence.text: Herbicide-tolerant GM crops increase herbicide use
thinEvidence.note: Herbicide-tolerant crops raised glyphosate use and drove resistant weeds, while Bt crops cut insecticide use.

thinEvidence.text: Knowing and trusting the farmer can replace organic certification
thinEvidence.note: Whether personal trust substitutes for third-party verification is a judgment about the buyer's values and knowledge.

thinEvidence.text: Organic farming cannot feed the world's current population
thinEvidence.note: About half of food output depends on synthetic nitrogen; models suggest an organic world is feasible only with large cuts in waste and animal feed.

thinEvidence.text: Organic food tastes better than conventional food
thinEvidence.note: Blind taste tests show no consistent preference for organic; label-aware tests show a halo effect.

thinEvidence.text: The USDA organic standard has been watered down as large companies entered organic
thinEvidence.note: Hydroponic certification and the 2018 withdrawal of the animal welfare rule are cited as weakening, but other rules such as pasture and enforcement were tightened.

thinEvidence.text: Fat-soluble pesticides and pollutants in the diet come mostly from animal foods
thinEvidence.note: Persistent organochlorines, dioxins and PCBs build up in animal fat, and most dietary exposure comes from meat, dairy and fish.

thinEvidence.text: Genetically engineered foods carry long-term health risks
thinEvidence.note: Major scientific reviews find no evidence that approved GE foods pose greater health risks than conventional foods.

thinEvidence.text: A global shift to organic farming could not feed the world without major diet changes
thinEvidence.note: Modelling studies find a fully organic system needs much more land and faces nitrogen shortfalls unless diets shift and food waste falls.

thinEvidence.text: A grass-fed label does not guarantee the animal was raised on pasture
thinEvidence.note: Generic grass-fed claims describe diet and are approved company by company; only some third-party certifiers also require pasture.

thinEvidence.text: Group certification lets most farms in foreign organic grower groups go uninspected by accredited certifiers
thinEvidence.note: Under older rules certifiers inspected only a sample of group members and relied on internal control systems; the 2024 enforcement rule tightened this.

thinEvidence.text: Healthy soil from organic farming produces healthier food and healthier people
thinEvidence.note: Soil health gains are measurable, but evidence linking organic soil management to better human health outcomes is lacking.

thinEvidence.text: Heavy glyphosate use has bred glyphosate-resistant superweeds
thinEvidence.note: Dozens of weed species have evolved glyphosate resistance, documented widely in Roundup Ready cropping systems.

thinEvidence.text: Many leading organic brands are owned by large conventional food companies
thinEvidence.note: Well-known US organic brands are owned by General Mills, Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, Kellogg, Danone and similar firms.

thinEvidence.text: Non-GMO labels often appear on foods that have no genetically engineered version
thinEvidence.note: Only a handful of crops have commercial GE varieties, yet non-GMO claims appear on many products that could never be genetically engineered.

thinEvidence.text: Organic certification has conflicts of interest because farms choose and pay their own certifiers
thinEvidence.note: Operations do choose and pay accredited certifiers, a structural conflict, though USDA accredits and audits the certifiers.

thinEvidence.text: Organic farming requires more labour than conventional farming
thinEvidence.note: Weeding and pest control without herbicides raise labour per hectare on most organic farms.

thinEvidence.text: Organic price premiums give sellers an incentive to pass off conventional food as organic
thinEvidence.note: Prosecuted fraud cases show sellers relabelling conventional grain and produce as organic to capture the premium.

thinEvidence.text: Organic rules rest on an appeal to nature rather than evidence of best practice
thinEvidence.note: This is a framing judgment about the philosophy behind organic standards.

thinEvidence.text: Pasture-raised is an unregulated term with no required outdoor standard
thinEvidence.note: USDA has no codified pasture-raised standard; meaning depends on producer claims unless a third-party certification backs it.

thinEvidence.text: Pre-harvest glyphosate spraying leaves higher residues in oats, grains and legumes
thinEvidence.note: Desiccant use close to harvest is the main reason conventional oats and pulses test higher for glyphosate, usually still within legal limits.

thinEvidence.text: USDA Organic standards do not protect farmworker welfare
thinEvidence.note: The National Organic Program regulates inputs and practices, not labour conditions or wages.

thinEvidence.text: Abruptly banning synthetic fertilizer sharply cuts crop yields
thinEvidence.note: Sri Lanka's 2021 fertilizer ban was followed by steep rice and tea output falls and was reversed within months.

thinEvidence.text: Animal Welfare Approved certification sets stronger hen welfare standards than USDA egg labels
thinEvidence.note: AWA requires pasture access, space minimums and bans beak cutting, well beyond USDA cage-free, free-range or organic rules.

thinEvidence.text: Conventional livestock are fed sewage sludge
thinEvidence.note: Biosolids are spread on some cropland and pasture under EPA rules, but they are not fed to livestock as feed.

thinEvidence.text: Dietary pesticide residues alter the human gut microbiome
thinEvidence.note: Animal studies and one small observational twin study suggest effects, but there is no causal human evidence.

thinEvidence.text: Genetically engineered crops are nutritionally equivalent to their conventional counterparts
thinEvidence.note: Compositional studies reviewed by the National Academies found approved GE crops nutritionally equivalent to conventional ones, apart from deliberately altered traits.

thinEvidence.text: Genetically engineered crops are as safe to eat as conventionally bred crops
thinEvidence.note: The 2016 National Academies review found no evidence that approved engineered crops are less safe to eat.

thinEvidence.text: Glyphosate in food drove the rise in celiac disease and gluten sensitivity
thinEvidence.note: Celiac disease is a genetic autoimmune condition; the glyphosate link rests on an ecological time-trend correlation, and rising celiac rates predate 2006.

thinEvidence.text: Grain-fed beef harms health in ways grass-fed beef does not
thinEvidence.note: No outcome studies show grass-fed beef eaters fare better; fat-profile differences are small relative to total diet.

thinEvidence.text: The grass-fed label lets producers set their own definition
thinEvidence.note: USDA withdrew its grass-fed marketing standard in 2016; FSIS approves label claims case by case on producer documentation.

thinEvidence.text: Growing your own vegetables improves physical and mental health
thinEvidence.note: Gardening studies show modest gains in activity and wellbeing, mostly from observational and small trials.

thinEvidence.text: Herbicide-tolerant GM crops are sprayed with glyphosate, leaving residues in the food
thinEvidence.note: Glyphosate-tolerant crops are sprayed and can carry residues, though highly refined products such as oils and sugar contain little.

thinEvidence.text: Hormones used in conventional beef and dairy raise cancer risk and cause early puberty
thinEvidence.note: Residues from approved beef implants and rbST are tiny next to natural hormone levels, and no causal link to cancer or early puberty is established.

thinEvidence.text: US law does not require genetically engineered foods to be labelled
thinEvidence.note: Since 2022 the National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard has required disclosure of bioengineered foods, though with exemptions.

thinEvidence.text: Modern crops contain far fewer vitamins and minerals than crops grown decades ago
thinEvidence.note: Historical comparisons show modest declines in some minerals, mostly from high-yield varieties, nowhere near several-fold losses.

thinEvidence.text: Most conventional grain crops are sprayed with glyphosate before harvest
thinEvidence.note: Pre-harvest desiccation is used on a minority of US wheat and on oats mainly in Canada, not on most corn or soy.

thinEvidence.text: Most grass-fed beef sold in the US is imported
thinEvidence.note: Industry analyses have estimated that most US grass-fed beef at retail comes from Australia, New Zealand and South America.

thinEvidence.text: Organic certification inspections are often cursory
thinEvidence.note: Inspection depth varies by certifier and inspector, and there is no systematic measure of how thorough organic inspections are.

thinEvidence.text: Organic dairy cows emit more methane than conventional dairy cows
thinEvidence.note: Forage-heavy diets raise methane per unit of milk in many studies, but per-cow and per-farm comparisons are mixed.

thinEvidence.text: Organic egg farms can meet outdoor-access rules with enclosed porches rather than pasture
thinEvidence.note: Porches have counted as outdoor access, but a 2023 USDA rule requires soil and vegetation outdoors, phased in by 2029 for existing farms.

thinEvidence.text: Organic eggs can carry more dioxin because hens forage outdoors
thinEvidence.note: Several European surveys found higher dioxin levels in free-range and organic eggs, usually still within legal limits.

thinEvidence.text: Organic eggs carry fewer pesticide residues because the hens eat organic feed
thinEvidence.note: Organic feed lowers pesticide inputs, but residues in conventional eggs are already rare and very low.

thinEvidence.text: Organic farmers are more exposed to price shocks than conventional farmers
thinEvidence.note: Organic premiums collapsed with inflation in 2022-23, though organic farms also receive specific EU subsidies.

thinEvidence.text: Organic farming relies on more tillage, which can degrade soil
thinEvidence.note: Organic weed control often uses more tillage, which can harm soil structure, though organic systems still tend to have higher soil organic matter.

thinEvidence.text: Organic farmland in France shrank after 2022 as farmers dropped certification
thinEvidence.note: French Agence Bio data show certified organic area fell from 2022 to 2024 as some farms deconverted.

thinEvidence.text: Organic food spoils faster than conventional food
thinEvidence.note: Few GM crops are engineered for shelf life, and studies find no consistent shelf-life difference attributable to organic production.

thinEvidence.text: An organic label leads people to underestimate a food's calories
thinEvidence.note: Experiments on the organic halo show people rate organic-labelled snacks as lower in calories.

thinEvidence.text: Organic meat has similar or higher greenhouse gas emissions than conventional meat
thinEvidence.note: Life-cycle studies generally find organic meat's emissions per kilogram similar to or above conventional meat because of slower growth and more land use.

thinEvidence.text: Organic product labels must be approved by an accredited certifier before use
thinEvidence.note: Under the NOP rules, certifiers review and approve organic labels as part of certification.

thinEvidence.text: The organic seal is most useful when buyers cannot know the farm
thinEvidence.note: This is shopping advice about when third-party verification adds value.

thinEvidence.text: Pasture-raised egg labels mean hens spend most of the day outdoors with ample space
thinEvidence.note: There is no USDA definition of pasture-raised; only third-party certifications such as Certified Humane set outdoor space and time rules.

thinEvidence.text: Plants cannot tell synthetic nitrogen from organic nitrogen
thinEvidence.note: Plants take up mineral nitrate and ammonium whatever the source, though organic inputs also change soil structure and release timing.

thinEvidence.text: A PLU code beginning with 8 identifies genetically engineered produce
thinEvidence.note: The 8 prefix was never adopted for GE produce, and IFPS has since dropped it and reassigns 8-series codes to new items.

thinEvidence.text: A PLU code beginning with 9 identifies organic produce
thinEvidence.note: Under the IFPS convention, a 9 prefix on a four-digit PLU marks organic produce, though use is voluntary.

thinEvidence.text: Post-harvest coatings that extend shelf life are allowed on organic produce
thinEvidence.note: At least one plant-lipid shelf-life coating has an organic-approved formulation, and coatings from allowed substances can be used on organic produce.

thinEvidence.text: Real Organic Project certification adds requirements beyond USDA Organic, such as banning hydroponics and animal confinement
thinEvidence.note: Real Organic Project is an add-on to USDA Organic that requires soil-grown crops and pasture-based livestock.

thinEvidence.text: Rice-based foods carry more inorganic arsenic than most other foods
thinEvidence.note: Rice takes up arsenic from flooded paddies far more than other grains, which is why FDA set a specific limit for infant rice cereal.

thinEvidence.text: Routine residue testing does not check for most pesticides used in organic farming
thinEvidence.note: The Pesticide Data Program tests hundreds of compounds including some used in organic, but it does not measure substances such as copper and sulfur.

thinEvidence.text: Some large certified organic dairies have violated pasture requirements
thinEvidence.note: The USDA has cited large organic dairies for pasture violations, and investigative reporting has found big herds with little grazing.

thinEvidence.text: Taking glycine supplements protects the body from glyphosate
thinEvidence.note: There is no human evidence that supplemental glycine blocks glyphosate uptake or effects.

thinEvidence.text: Ultra-pasteurization strips milk of much of its nutritional value
thinEvidence.note: UHT causes modest losses of some heat-sensitive vitamins but leaves protein, calcium and most nutrients largely intact.

thinEvidence.text: Virtually no US retail milk comes from rBST-treated cows, so rBST-free labels add nothing
thinEvidence.note: Use of rBST has fallen to a small minority of herds and most processors refuse it, but it is still approved and not entirely gone.
